newsitem.title: USA: White House - NATO expansion can work for Russia.
newsitem.headline: White House - NATO expansion can work for Russia.

text.p: The White House on Tuesday restated its support for NATO expansion, in response to the Russian prime minister's published fears of "ominous" results if the alliance expands to include central Europe.

"Our course of action has been determined," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters who asked about a published interview with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin. "The point is to make it work and to make it work for all nations, including the Russian Federation."
In an interview published on Tuesday in the Washington Post, Chernomyrdin said NATO expansion would fuel extremist demands in Russia for a return to armed confrontation with the West.

"I'm worried about Russia," Chernomyrdin told the paper. The West "wants us to explain to our people that there is nothing to fear. How can we explain this? Nobody is going to listen to any explanations ... Developments in Russia could take an ominous turn."
Chernomyrdin said he would warn President Bill Clinton that rapid expansion of NATO into central Europe could undermine the government of President Boris Yeltsin.
McCurry said Chernomyrdin's statements were "very simlar to what (Russian officials) have been saying publicly and we have taken our decision on the question of the future of NATO."

Asked about Chernomyrdin's demand that NATO sign with Russia "a binding treaty, with verification" to change NATO from a military body into "a political organisation" that would not treat Russia as its main threat and enemy, McCurry said the matter could come up in this week's talks between Chernomyrdin and Vice President Al Gore.

"I anticipate a lot of discussion on the issue of NATO expansion when the president sees President Yeltsin and one of the purposes of the upcoming Gore-Chernomyrdin meeting is to structure the discussion that the two presidents will have," McCurry told reporters.
The Kremlin has been critical of plans by the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation to take in new members from among Moscow's former Warsaw Pact allies.
NATO plans at its July summit to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to become members two years from now.
Chernomyrdin said he would press his position in talks with Gore on Wednesday and Thursday and with Clinton on Friday.
NATO has already rejected this proposal.
Chernomyrdin portrayed the U.S.-Russian relationship as being at a significant turning point, the Post reported.

He suggested that failure to resolve the NATO expansion issue by the time Clinton and Yeltsin are due to meet in March could lead to civil unrest within Russia "and the tanks will be rolling out" of now inactive factories.

Chernomyrdin said he favours shifting the summit to Europe to conserve Yeltsin's strength. He said he feared ultranationalists like Vladimir Zhirinovsky "will accuse the president and the government of doing nothing to prevent" the NATO expansion.
McCurry said he had no information on the time or place of the Clinton-Yeltsin meeting.
